title: publish-release.sh guarantees wrapper-after-platforms by ORDER, but npm visibility is per-package -- 0.7.0 left a 121s window where the wrapper resolved and two platform packages did not
description:
THE SCRIPT'S ORDERING GUARANTEE IS FALSE AS STATED, AND 0.7.0 PROVES IT.

scripts/publish-release.sh:637 promises: "stopping BEFORE the root launcher, so the launcher never
resolves to a binary that is not there." Line 49 says the same. THE GUARANTEE IS ABOUT PUBLISH ORDER.
THE PROPERTY THAT MATTERS IS VISIBILITY ORDER. They are not the same thing and 0.7.0 separated them.

=== WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED ON 0.7.0, MEASURED ===

The script's own visibility poll, in order of becoming resolvable:

  darwin-arm64   0s
  linux-x64      0s
  win32-x64      1s
  darwin-x64    79s
  lore          79s   <-- THE WRAPPER BECAME RESOLVABLE HERE
  win32-arm64  140s
  linux-arm64  200s   <-- 121 SECONDS AFTER THE WRAPPER

So for roughly two minutes, `@opum-ai/lore@0.7.0` resolved on the registry while
`@opum-ai/lore-linux-arm64@0.7.0` and `@opum-ai/lore-win32-arm64@0.7.0` did not. That is precisely
the state the guarantee claims cannot occur.

THE PLATFORM PACKAGES ARE optionalDependencies, and the wrapper declares NO hard dependencies
(verified: `npm view @opum-ai/lore@0.7.0 optionalDependencies` lists all six; `dependencies` is
empty). So an install inside that window does not fail loudly -- IT SUCCEEDS WITH THE BINARY
MISSING. That is the worse of the two failure shapes: a silent bad install rather than a refusal.

=== CREDIT, AND A MECHANISM CORRECTION WORTH KEEPING ===

FOUND BY opum-cli-e2e, 2026-09-15, by polling all fourteen packages of the pair instead of trusting
a publish report. They read the per-package publish timestamps from the packument:

  lore-darwin-arm64  12:27:18.928Z
  lore-linux-x64     12:27:38.891Z
  lore-win32-x64     12:27:52.692Z
  lore (WRAPPER)     12:28:49.026Z
  lore-darwin-x64    12:29:05.007Z
  lore-win32-arm64   12:29:26.821Z
  lore-linux-arm64   12:30:13.383Z

and concluded the wrapper was PUBLISHED 84s before the last platform package.

THAT INFERENCE IS WRONG, AND THE CORRECTION MATTERS BECAUSE IT CHANGES THE FIX. The script cannot
have published the wrapper fourth: publish_one is called in a `for` loop over PLATFORM_PKGS that
`break`s on failure, then `die`s, and ROOT_PKG is published on the line AFTER that die. The control
flow makes wrapper-last unconditional. Nor does the packument order match the script's actual
publish order, which is alphabetical by platform (darwin-arm64, darwin-x64, linux-arm64, linux-x64,
win32-arm64, win32-x64).

What the packument order DOES match, position for position, is the visibility order above -- the two
agree on all seven, with the only discrepancy being lore and darwin-x64, which my poll could not
separate because it observed both in the same iteration at 79s. So `time[<version>]` tracks REGISTRY
PROCESSING, not the moment the PUT was issued.

THE CONCLUSION SURVIVES THE CORRECTED MECHANISM, AND IS WORSE FOR IT. The defect is not a fixable
ordering bug in the script's loop. Publishing last does not make a package visible last, because
propagation is per-package and bimodal (0s to 200s in this one release). ORDERING THE WRITES CANNOT
PRODUCE THE GUARANTEE AT ALL. Only gating on reads can.

=== WHY NOTHING CAUGHT THIS EARLIER ===

The script already HAS a visibility poll -- it added one for LCLI-460 -- but it runs AFTER all seven
publishes, as a precondition for the install smoke test. It is positioned as "wait before smoking",
not as "gate the wrapper". The information needed to prevent the window was already being collected
one step too late.

This is the same shape as LCLI-489 (the digest check that proves less than it appears to) and the
same lesson as this repo's standing rule that producing code is a hypothesis until checked against
the consuming side. A guarantee asserted in a die() message is not a tested property.

acceptanceCriteria.text: The root launcher is not published until all six platform packages are VISIBLE on the registry read API, not merely until their PUTs have returned -- the existing post-publish poll moved earlier and made a gate rather than a precondition for the smoke test. NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT: see the two constraints below, either of which leaves this wrong

STAGED IS A THIRD OUTCOME. npm 12 parks a version awaiting 2FA in a non-public state that still occupies the semver index, and it is INVISIBLE TO THE PUBLISHING TOKEN (`npm stage list` returned [] under quest`s own release token while a version was staged). A gate that only distinguishes published from missing converts a 2FA stall into an indefinite hang diagnosed as registry lag. Distinguish it by something other than the publisher`s own read

CONSUMER-VISIBLE LAGS REGISTRY-PROCESSED BY 0-20s, measured across five packages. A publisher-side poll reporting visible is early for an installer by that margin regardless of where it sits, so `the publisher can see it` is not the property either

scripts/publish-release.sh:49 and the die() at :637 stop claiming the launcher never resolves before its binary, or become true. A guarantee asserted in an error message and never tested is the defect this task exists to close

The release-truth record and the runbook state that npm packument time[<version>] tracks REGISTRY PROCESSING rather than PUT order, so the next reader does not re-derive the wrong mechanism from the same timestamps
A regression check exists: publishing with a deliberately delayed platform package must refuse to publish the launcher rather than proceeding

implementationNotes:
=== 0.6.2 HAD THE SAME WINDOW. THIS IS NOT A 0.7.0 REGRESSION -- IT IS A LATENT DEFECT SHIPPED TWICE ===

From opum-agent, 2026-09-15, after this task was filed. Their fleet memory already held the 0.6.2
version of the same measurement -- THREE packages absent, ~120s -- recorded under the conclusion
"It had not failed... release sound."

That conclusion was wrong in exactly the way this task identifies. The publish-ORDER invariant had
not failed. The property a user actually cares about -- that the wrapper never resolves before the
binary it execs -- HAD failed, in 0.6.2 as well as 0.7.0.

SO THE SCOPE IS WIDER THAN THE TITLE SUGGESTS. 0.7.0 is where it was detected, not where it began.
Every manual publish through scripts/publish-release.sh has had this window; 0.6.1 and 0.6.0 were
not measured and should be assumed affected rather than assumed clean. Nothing here is a regression
introduced by 0.7.0's changes.

=== IT WAS BELIEVED AND RECORDED TWICE BEFORE BEING SEEN ===

The weaker conclusion was drawn from sufficient data on two separate releases by two different
sessions. Worse, opum-agent's copy was in persistent fleet memory, actively teaching the next
session to dismiss this as a transient-404 nuisance. They have rewritten it around this task.

That is the part worth keeping: this defect's signature is a measurement that looks like an operator
hazard. THE COMFORTABLE READING IS "be careful when you see this". THE CORRECT READING IS "this
state is supposed to be impossible". A guarantee asserted in a die() message is not a tested
property, and nothing was testing this one.

=== RULING: 0.7.0 IS NOT BEING PULLED ===

opum-agent, tier-1 delivery scope, settled without escalation to the user. The window is closed, all
seven packages resolve, and `npm unpublish` is irreversible for 72 hours -- pulling would remove a
working package from users who now have a working install, to protect users in a window that no
longer exists. Anyone who did install inside those 121 seconds hit a missing binary immediately and
would reinstall. The remedy is this task's gate, in the next release.

=== THE FIND ALREADY PAID FOR ITSELF ON THE OTHER HALF OF THE PAIR ===

quest 0.7.0 had NOT published when this was found. opum-agent asked quest-cli to check, BEFORE
publishing, whether their path has the same shape -- platform packages first, wrapper last,
visibility polled only afterwards -- and whether their platform packages are likewise
optionalDependencies against a wrapper with no hard dependency. If so they can two-phase the publish
by hand and make the window structurally impossible.

They were advised to prefer the MANUAL two-phase over a script fix, on the ground that editing a
publish script minutes before using it puts an untested change in the one path that cannot be rolled
back. Worth recording as a general rule: do not fix the irreversible path under time pressure --
work around it by hand, then fix it with a test.

=== CREDIT WHERE IT BELONGS ===

Found because opum-cli-e2e polled all FOURTEEN packages of the pair rather than trusting the
publisher's report. Verifying a peer's claim caught a defect the peer's own tooling asserted was
impossible. That is what independent verification is for.

=== TWO CONSTRAINTS THAT BREAK THE OBVIOUS FIX. READ BEFORE IMPLEMENTING AC1. ===

From opum-cli-e2e, 2026-09-15, out of quest 0.7.0's publish. The naive reading of this task -- "poll
the registry before publishing the launcher" -- produces a gate that is STILL WRONG on both counts.

--- 1. STAGED IS A THIRD OUTCOME, AND IT IS INVISIBLE TO THE PUBLISHING TOKEN ---

`@opum-ai/quest-darwin-x64@0.7.0` was STAGED rather than published. npm 12 parks a version awaiting
a maintainer's 2FA in a non-public state that STILL OCCUPIES THE SEMVER INDEX. Consequences, all
observed:

  - their publish loop printed SUCCESS
  - the public packument had no 0.7.0
  - `npm stage list` under their own release token returned `[]`

For about eleven minutes the quest wrapper was live advertising a version no consumer could resolve.
It went public at 13:16:58.797Z once the 2FA was completed.

WHY THIS BREAKS THIS TASK'S FIX SPECIFICALLY: the gate AC1 describes runs with the PUBLISH
CREDENTIAL. On a staged version that gate reads "not yet visible" and waits -- for a window that
will never close on its own, because nothing is propagating. It would have converted an eleven-minute
2FA stall into an indefinite hang, diagnosed as registry lag. The publisher's own tooling could not
have told anyone why.

SO THE GATE NEEDS THREE OUTCOMES, NOT TWO: published, missing, and STAGED. And staged must be
distinguished by something OTHER than the publisher's own read, since that is precisely the view it
is invisible to. That `npm stage list` returned `[]` under the release token while a version was
staged is the detail that makes this a design constraint rather than a footnote.

--- 2. CONSUMER-VISIBLE LAGS REGISTRY-PROCESSED BY 0-20 SECONDS ---

Measured by opum-cli-e2e across five packages. A publisher-side poll reporting "visible" is EARLY
FOR AN INSTALLER by that margin, independently of where the poll sits in the script.

So "the publisher can see it" is not the property either. Moving the existing poll earlier -- the
minimal reading of AC1 -- closes most of the window and leaves 0-20 seconds of it, in exactly the
shape that is hardest to reproduce and easiest to call a flake.

--- WHAT THIS MEANS FOR AC1 ---

AC1 says "VISIBLE on the registry read API, not merely until their PUTs have returned". That wording
is necessary and not sufficient. An implementation satisfying it literally, using the publish
credential, still hangs forever on a staged version and still ships a 0-20s window to installers.
Do not close this task on a poll-moved-earlier patch.

=== PROVENANCE OF THESE FINDINGS ===

Both came from opum-cli-e2e checking rather than from either publisher's tooling -- the same session
that found the original defect here by polling all fourteen packages instead of trusting the
publishers' reports. That is now TWICE in one release that the real defect came from independent
verification and not from the system that owned the code. Worth weighting when deciding how much
qualification a release deserves.

lore's own seven published cleanly and hit neither issue. This is recorded because lore's publish
path has the SAME SHAPE, not because lore hit it -- the difference was timing, not design.

=== A MECHANISM CORRECTION ON THE STAGED-STATE CONSTRAINT, FROM ITS OWN SOURCE ===

opum-cli-e2e, 2026-09-15, correcting a stronger claim they had made to me earlier. Recorded because
if `time.modified` ends up in this task's gate, the difference decides whether the gate is sound.

WHAT `time.modified` ACTUALLY DISTINGUISHES: "the PUBLIC PACKUMENT was not written" from "nothing
happened". IT DOES NOT PROVE NOTHING WAS WRITTEN ANYWHERE -- which is precisely what staging turned
out to be. A staged version IS written; it just is not written where an unauthenticated consumer, or
the publishing token's own read, can see it.

So as a gate instrument it is SHARPER THAN A `versions` READ and BLUNTER than first asserted. Usable,
but it cannot by itself tell staged from missing. Their operative conclusion at the time held -- the
release was incomplete for consumers and holding was right -- but the mechanism asserted for it did
not, and the mechanism is what an implementer would build on.

THE SHARPEST STATEMENT OF WHY THIS TASK'S GATE IS HARD, in their words and better than mine: the
publisher's own tooling could not distinguish WAITING FOR PROPAGATION from WAITING FOR A HUMAN WHO
HAS NOT BEEN ASKED -- and it would have kept waiting. Three outcomes, and the third is only visible
from OUTSIDE the publishing credential. A gate built on any single publisher-side read, `time.modified`
included, cannot separate them.

=== WHY THIS NOTE EXISTS AT ALL ===

Two sessions in this release each asserted a mechanism confidently, had it corrected, and found the
CONCLUSION survived while the mechanism did not: their packument-timestamps-as-publish-order, and
this. Mine went the other way -- my conclusion was the weak one and the data was already sufficient.
The pattern worth carrying is that a conclusion and the mechanism offered for it fail independently,
so confirming one is not confirming the other. Check the mechanism before building on it, even when
the conclusion it came with was right.

lore's own seven published cleanly and hit none of this. Recorded because lore's publish path has
the same shape, not because lore hit it.

SESSION HANDOFF 2026-09-15. STANDING USER RULING RECORDED HERE BECAUSE THIS TASK IS THE GATE.

THE RULING, asked and answered directly by the owner via AskUserQuestion on
2026-09-15: WAIT. No lore 0.7.1 is cut until LCLI-502, LCLI-510 and LCLI-507 land.
Do not re-litigate it and do not re-ask on a spec improvement.

THE QUESTION THAT PROMPTED IT, so the successor does not re-derive it: quest
published 0.7.1 and lore is at 0.7.0, and the orchestrator asked whether a matching
lore 0.7.1 was warranted. Measured answer: of the 13 commits since v0.7.0 exactly
ONE touches src/ -- LCLI-503, which changes status-flow ERROR TEXT so it names the
active backend instead of hardcoding backlog/config.yml. Real, user-facing, and
minor. Ten of thirteen touch only .quest/. That is not worth a release on its own.

WHY THIS TASK SPECIFICALLY GATES IT, and it is the strongest of the three reasons:
publishing again before this is fixed REOPENS the window this task describes. 0.7.0
left ~121s where the wrapper resolved and two platform packages did not, and
because the platform packages are optionalDependencies an install inside that
window SUCCEEDS WITH THE BINARY MISSING rather than failing. A silent success is
worse than a loud failure. LCLI-510 would ship a stale npm page again; LCLI-507 is
the CI flake that makes a release run likelier to need re-runs.

RIDE-ALONGS when a 0.7.1 eventually is cut, neither justifying one on its own:
LCLI-503 (already landed on dev) and LCLI-512 (export help advertises schema 1.0
and ships an example that fails; the exporter writes 1.1).

THE SECOND STANDING RULING, recorded in full on LCLI-500 and pointed at from here
because the two are usually considered together: the npm publish token rotation is
DEFERRED, third deferral, chosen directly by the owner the same day. Its note
states the condition that makes it tolerable AND the condition that expires it --
no publish is imminent, so the deferral does not currently sit in front of a
registry write, and when a 0.7.1 IS cut the question goes live again and must be
RE-ASKED rather than inherited from that answer. Cutting a release under this task
is therefore the exact moment to re-ask it.

Isolation correction mid-task: initial work landed uncommitted in the shared root (which had another agent's branch checked out) before I created .claude/worktrees/lcli-502 on fix/LCLI-502-publish-visibility-gate and moved my edits there by hand. All commits/PR come from the isolated worktree.

AC1+AC3 implemented: added a 'REGISTRY GATE BEFORE THE ROOT LAUNCHER' block that calls wait_for_all_visible() over the six platform packages BEFORE publish_one(ROOT_PKG), then sleeps PROPAGATION_CUSHION_SECONDS=20 (documented, cites opum-cli-e2e's 0-20s external measurement) before publishing root. Skipped entirely under --dry-run so existing dry-run tests stay fast/side-effect-free.

AC2 (staged/2FA) investigated via source, not guessed: read npm@12.0.2's own shipped source (lib/commands/publish.js, lib/commands/stage/{index,publish}.js, node_modules/libnpmpublish/lib/publish.js, node_modules/npm-registry-fetch/lib/{check-response,index}.js, lib/utils/auth.js) and its docs (docs/content/commands/npm-stage.md), all installed at ~/.nvm/versions/node/v24.20.0/lib/node_modules/npm on this machine. Finding, cited in a comment in the script above looks_like_2fa_or_staging(): staging is reachable only via the distinct 'npm stage publish' verb or a trust-relationship/OIDC token; this script uses neither (Keychain/NPM_TOKEN GAT-with-bypass, or ~/.npmrc session-token fallback), so a live silent-success-while-staged could NOT be reproduced against this script's own credential paths. Built the detection as a pluggable hook per the task's own fallback clause: looks_like_2fa_or_staging() scans each npm publish call's captured stdout+stderr for EOTP / 'one-time pass' / '(staged' (verified strings/codes from npm's own source), and the shared wait_for_all_visible() timeout message now tells an operator to check 'npm stage list <pkg>' (noting it can itself report nothing under a restricted token type -- also from npm's docs) and npmjs.com directly, rather than presenting a stall as ordinary propagation lag.

AC4: corrected the false publish-ORDER guarantee in the script header (safety properties bullet) and in the platform-loop die() message, and in docs/runbooks/release-publishing.md's parallel claim ('so the launcher is never resolvable before the binary it execs'). All three now describe the registry-visibility gate + cushion instead of publish order.

AC5: added corrected passages to docs/reference/lore-cli-release-truth.md (Current state section, three new paragraphs after 'Publish order is not propagation order') stating the 121s 0.7.0 window, the packument time[<version>]-tracks-processing-not-PUT-order correction, and the staged/2FA investigation result; and to docs/runbooks/release-publishing.md's step describing the script. lore sync + lore check both run clean (see final report).

AC6: added a non-dry-run regression test (test/publish-release-script.test.ts, 'holds the root launcher until a delayed platform package is registry-visible, not merely published (LCLI-502)') with a custom npm stub that delays ONE platform package's registry visibility by one poll and logs every view/publish call in order; asserts root's npm publish call index is after the delayed package's observed MISS-then-HIT transition. Passes; full suite (bun test) green at 3156 pass / 1 skip / 0 fail after bun install v1.3.14 (0d9b296a)

Checked 113 installs across 119 packages (no changes) [23.00ms] in the fresh worktree.
finalSummary: Fixed in PR #131 (opum-ai/lore-cli, fix/LCLI-502-publish-visibility-gate). Root launcher publish is now gated on registry-read visibility of all six platform packages plus a documented 20s propagation cushion (AC1, AC3), not merely publish order. Added a pluggable, documented staged/2FA detection hook after investigating npm@12.0.2's own shipped source and docs -- staging is reachable only via 'npm stage publish' or a trust-relationship/OIDC credential, neither of which this script uses, so a live silent-success-while-staged could not be reproduced against this script's own credential paths; that limitation is stated in the code comment rather than overclaimed (AC2). Corrected the false publish-order guarantee in the script header, its die() message, and the runbook (AC4), and corrected docs/reference/lore-cli-release-truth.md with the 121s 0.7.0 window and the packument time[<version>]-is-processing-not-PUT-order mechanism correction (AC5). Added a non-dry-run regression test proving publish ordering via a call log, not just absence of a crash (AC6). Evidence: bun test 3156 pass/1 skip/0 fail, bun run typecheck clean, bun run lint clean, bash scripts/lint-shell.sh clean, lore check 79 files/0 errors/0 warnings.
